contract.journey: Create + edit glossary translation in BO.

name: Glossary
rationale: Back-office half ported: create a translation, see it listed, edit it, read the change back off the form. The storefront half is deliberately not ported - it edited a translation key the storefront renders and undid it in a teardown, and Cypress shards pack nondeterministically, so a spec rendering that page in a neighbouring shard would race with the edit. No CI run URL: the only focused run that covered this spec is red for it - it edited whichever row the table happened to be showing, passing once and failing twice on retry. The list page now asserts the key is in the table before taking a row, and the local green post-dates that fix. The next full dispatch supersedes this record.
target_test: should create a translation and list it

contract.journey: Checks customer data and checkout as an agent.

name: Agent_Assist
rationale: Needed new storefront impersonation support, which nothing in cypress-tests had. The agent control bar has to be driven rather than short-circuited: the visible search field carries no name and the form submits a hidden _switch_user input that the autocomplete fills, so the suggestion has to be clicked. Only the older agent-control-bar component exists in this package version, so the two UI generations the Robot keyword branches on collapse to one. The same support unblocks both company rows. Coverage is not the five interchangeable clones the variant count suggests: only the suite and b2c sources place an order, while the b2b, mp_b2b and mp_b2c sources stop at the product detail page. Those three - and b2c as well - assert that impersonation carries the customer's own price context, the impersonated customer's price on the catalog listing and again on the PDP, and for b2b and mp_b2b that price assertion is the whole delta over what impersonating at all already proves. The port asserts no price, and no other Cypress spec asserts one under impersonation, so deleting those clones drops it. b2c's order-history read-back is unported too; the port asserts the order-placed message instead. The checkout test is skipped on b2b and b2b-mp, which is source parity rather than a narrowing - neither clone opened the cart, and the fixture builds no company user, so the b2b cart permissions are absent. Widening means the price assertions plus, for a b2b order, the company, business unit, role and company-user chain - out of scope for this batch, and recorded here so the cutover does not take these five clones for one test. No CI run URL: the focused run that covered this spec is red overall - the spec itself passed in it, but two unrelated specs in one shard did not, so linking it would send a reader to a failure. The next full dispatch supersedes this record.
target_test: agent should be able to place an order for the impersonated customer

contract.journey: Create a user with limited access.

name: User_Control
rationale: Delta only: acl-navigation-access.cy.ts already covers allow and deny at navigation and path level. The delta landed as two tests in that same spec, 'should deny an action for a role with an explicit deny rule' and 'should refuse login for a deactivated user'; target_test names the first. Coverage narrows to suite: that spec self-skips unless repositoryId is suite, a guard predating this port, and its ACL fixture exists only under cypress/fixtures/suite. The Robot source is a real clone in all five shops, so deleting the b2b, b2c, mp_b2b and mp_b2c clones drops the journey there. Widening it means building the ACL role, rule and group fixtures for the four demoshops and lifting the guard - out of scope for this batch, and it is recorded here so the cutover does not take the narrowing for a clean swap. Verified in CI: shard 3 of 5 of that run ran the spec as 4 tests, 4 passing, so both new tests are CI-proven rather than only locally green. Re-proven locally as 4 passing in 22s. The port also drops a surface, not only four shops. The source builds its whole fixture through the back office - /acl/role then Add new Role for the role, the bundle/controller/action selects once for an allow rule and once for a deny rule, the group form with the role attached, the user form including the agent-in-Storefront checkbox and the interface locale, and finally the deactivate row action before the refused login. The port replaces all of it with the haveRole, haveRule, haveGroup, addRoleToGroup, haveUser and addUserToGroup helpers. Two of those surfaces survive elsewhere in cypress-tests: the user create form, driven by UserMfaCreateScenario from the back-office MFA spec, and the agent-in-Storefront checkbox, asserted by the marketplace agent-permission spec. Three do not. Nothing in the repository reaches /acl/role or /acl/group - the only ACL path is /acl/index/denied - so role creation, allow/deny rule assignment and group creation with a role lose their last UI coverage. Nor does anything deactivate a user: UserIndexPage.update accepts the deactivate action and no spec passes it, so 'should refuse login for a deactivated user' asserts the blocked state a fixture handed it rather than the transition into it. Both users.robot scenarios are in this batch, so no sibling row keeps those forms alive after the cutover. Widening means an ACL role, rule and group page-object set plus a deactivate step in the login test - out of scope for this batch, and recorded here so the cutover does not read this row as a like-for-like swap.
target_test: should deny an action for a role with an explicit deny rule

contract.journey: Bug: https://spryker.atlassian.net/browse/CC-12380.

name: Unique_URL
rationale: New spec. Nothing in cypress-tests drove the share-cart-by-link widget, so CartPage gained getExternalCartShareLink and all five cart repositories gained the two selectors behind it. The widget renders one url-mask-generator per share option group; clicking that group's toggler fires the cart/create-link AJAX and the generated link is rendered into an input whose id is the share option itself, PREVIEW for the external group, so the toggler is reached through url-mask-generator[shareoptiongroup=external] and the link read from #PREVIEW. The journey's whole point is that the link works for someone who is not signed in, so the spec logs the customer out before visiting it and asserts the preview title and the product on the resulting page. The cart is seeded as a named persistent quote rather than created through the UI, which is what makes the expected 'Preview: <name>' title deterministic. Narrowed to the company-account storefronts: sharing a cart by link is a multiple-carts feature and the B2C shops do not carry it, which matches the source's own variant set of b2b, mp_b2b and suite. Not ported: the source's creation of the cart through the storefront and its dms-on tag, neither of which the shared-link behaviour depends on.
target_test: given a cart shared by external link when an anonymous visitor opens it then the cart is shown as a read-only preview

contract.journey: Checks role permissions on checkout and Approval process.

name: Approval_Process
rationale: New spec. Nothing in cypress-tests drove the quote-approval process, so CheckoutSummaryPage gained the approver select, the send-request and cancel-request handles, and CartPage gained the approver's approve action plus the locked-cart marker. The controls are spread across two surfaces and three path shapes, which is the part worth recording: the request is sent from the checkout summary at /quote-approval/create, the requester's cancel sits on the same page at /quote-approval/<id>/remove with the id between the segments, and the approver's approve and decline are on the cart page at /quote-approval/approve/<id> with the id trailing - not on the summary, despite the source's wording, as the glossary key quote_approval_widget.cart.approve confirms. None of them carries a data-qa, so the path is the handle. The buyer's spend limit is configuration on PlaceOrderPermissionPlugin itself rather than a separate plugin: there is no PlaceOrderWithAmountUpToPermissionPlugin registered on suite, and the cap is store_multi_currency.DE.EUR in cents on the permission attached to the role. Two conditions had to be met before the widget appeared at all: an active company user, without which the storefront has no company context and no limit applies, and a cart above the cap. A cart waiting for approval is shared with the approver but is not their active cart, so every leg selects this run's cart out of the multi-cart list by name - both customers accumulate carts across runs, and without that the outcome depended on whichever stale cart happened to be active. Assertions follow the source: status Waiting with the cancel-request form offered, the cart locked while it waits, status Approved after the approver acts, and the order placed by the buyer afterwards. Not ported: the source's second and third carts, which prove that an under-limit cart still orders directly and that a second waiting cart is untouched by approving the first. Both are isolation checks around the same mechanism rather than the mechanism itself, and each needs its own cart and checkout pass; recorded here so the cutover does not read this row as covering them.
target_test: given a cart above the buyer spend limit when the approver approves the request then the buyer can place the order

contract.journey: Guest checkout with discounts, OMS and different addresses.

name: Guest_Checkout_and_Addresses
rationale: Duplicate journey — retired by the port of checkout/Guest_Checkout_Addresses; delete it in that sibling's batch, it needs no port of its own. Also folds into checkout/Guest_Checkout; both siblings together cover this journey.

contract.journey: Checks that business unit address can be used during checkout.

name: Business_Unit_Address_on_Checkout
rationale: New spec. The source deletes the customer's own addresses so that the only address checkout can offer is the business unit's; the port gets there by giving the fixture customer no address at all, which is the same condition without a destructive setup step. Three things had to be true before the address appeared, and each fails quietly. The relation row is the first: spy_company_unit_address has no fk_company_business_unit column, the link lives in spy_company_unit_address_to_company_business_unit, and passing fkCompanyBusinessUnit to haveCompanyUnitAddress is accepted and does nothing. The relation helper is the second: it is typed CompanyBusinessUnitTransfer and the dynamic-fixture layer hands inline objects through as plain arrays, so the fixture has to build the transfer with a transfer operation carrying addressCollection.companyUnitAddresses and pass it by reference - referenced keys are hydrated into transfers, inline literals are not. An active company user is the third: without one the header reads 'No selected company' and the select offers only 'Define new address', so the spec selects the company user through CompanyUserSelectPage before opening the cart. Selecting the address needed a new handle too. For a plain customer the select is addressesForm_shippingAddress_id_customer_address, but with a company user active it renders with no id and name checkout-full-addresses; the class js-address__form-select-shippingAddress is on it in both layouts, so the new getShippingAddressSelectElement uses that, and the address is chosen by its option text because a business unit address carries no id_customer_address value. The fixture also uses only PlaceOrderPermissionPlugin: AddCartItemPermissionPlugin, which the b2b fixtures use freely, is unregistered on suite and makes havePermissionByKey return null, which fails the whole fixture load with an HTTP 500. Not ported: the source's named multi-cart, which no part of this journey depends on, and its literal expected address string, replaced by asserting the seeded street on the order details page.
target_test: given a company user with no personal address when the business unit address is chosen at checkout then the order ships to it

contract.journey: Bug: CC-30439. Checks that user can change address during the checkout and save new into the address book.

name: Checkout_Address_Management
rationale: New spec. The source guards a specific defect: a customer who enters a billing address, walks forward to a later checkout step, comes back to the address step and changes both addresses must end up with the second pair on the order, and only the address whose save-to-address-book box was ticked may appear in the address book. Nothing in cypress-tests could express that, because CheckoutAddressPage only ever filled a shipping address with billing-same-as-shipping ticked. It gained setBillingSameAsShipping, selectExistingShippingAddress, typeShippingAddress, typeBillingAddress, setShippingAddressSavedToAddressBook, setBillingAddressSavedToAddressBook and submitAddressStep, and all five repositories gained the two save-to-address-book checkboxes. Those checkboxes are labelled 'Save new address to address book' but bound to CheckoutAddressForm's isAddressSavingSkipped through an inverting model transformer, so checked means saved - the page method is named for the label, not the field. Returning to the address step is done by visiting it rather than by clicking the breadcrumb, which is the same navigation the source's 'return to the previous checkout step' keyword performs. Because the spec drives the steps itself instead of going through CheckoutScenario it also has to repeat that scenario's recurring-order/clear intercept; without it the summary renders correctly and the run simply never leaves /checkout/summary. Assertions: the address book contains the saved shipping street and neither billing street, and in the back office the order's billing address is the second billing address and the shipment's delivery address is the saved shipping one. SalesDetailRepository gained getBillingAddress, selected as the dd following the 'Billing address' dt since Sales renders it with no data-qa. Not ported: the source's country change to Switzerland, which only served to make the address visually distinct - the streets already do that - and its setup and teardown deleting all customer addresses, unnecessary against a per-run dynamic fixture customer.
target_test: given a separate billing address when the customer returns to the address step and changes both addresses then the order takes the changed ones and only the address marked for saving is added to the address book

contract.journey: checks that product offer is successfully replaced with a target product offer.

name: Click_and_collect
rationale: Now locally proven, after repairing the search index the service-point picker depends on. The checkout address step embeds ServicePointSearchWidget, which queries Elasticsearch, and the index had never been built from Spryker's schema - it was created implicitly by the first documents indexed, so it carried no analysis settings and completion-terms was a dynamically mapped text field. That is why search:setup:sources could not repair it in place, failing on the missing suggestion_analyzer. Deleting the spryker_* indices and re-running search:setup:sources rebuilds them from schema, after which the widget renders. The spec drives the single-shipment address form directly: a one-item cart never renders the multi-shipment trigger CheckoutScenario looks for, and the single-shipment form carries the shipment-type radios and its own service-point selector, so CheckoutAddressPage gained selectPickupAtServicePoint - the existing service-point getters were all per address item. Pickup offers no billing-same-as-shipping, since there is no shipping address to mirror, so the spec enters a billing address; ticking the checkbox instead leaves the form invalid and the run silently stays on the address step. Because the spec drives the steps itself it repeats CheckoutScenario's recurring-order intercept. Assertions verified against the data as well as the page: the placed order has one shipment and its sales-order-address row is the service point's own address, not the customer's. The whole Merchant Portal half of the source is replaced by fixtures rather than ported. The source authors a multi-SKU product and two offers through the Merchant Portal and approves the product in Zed before checking out; driving three surfaces to arrange one cart is setup rather than journey, and what the row's documentation claims is that a product offer is collected at a service point, which is the storefront half. Recorded here so the cutover does not read this row as covering Merchant Portal offer authoring or the Zed product approval action. Not ported either: the source's discount deactivation and reactivation teardown, which guards demo-data totals and has no equivalent need against per-run fixtures, and its assertion of a named Free Pickup shipping method, for the reason a sibling row records - the shipment radios carry the method's position rather than its name.
target_test: given an offer collected at a service point when the order is placed then it ships to the service point as a single pickup shipment

contract.journey: Editing and deleting comments in carts.

name: Comment_Management_in_the_Cart
rationale: Add, edit and delete a cart comment with a visibility assertion after each step — identical to the Cypress cart-comment edit and remove tests; the highest-scoring pair in the duplication report.

contract.journey: Add comments to cart and verify comments in Yves and Zed.

name: Comments_in_Cart
rationale: Delta only: adding a cart comment is covered by the six tests already in this spec; what is left is the comment surviving checkout and appearing on the Yves order-details page and in the back office. Landed as a seventh test there. The fixture gained a rootUser plus addUserToGroup so the order can be read back in the back office, and a commentToKeepThroughCheckout static message distinct from the six the other tests use. The back-office assertion is the part worth recording: the order page carries two unrelated comment boxes, and asserting on the wrong one fails with the comment plainly present in the database. Sales' own box renders .order-details-chat from spy_sales_order_comment, which only a Zed user writes to; the customer's cart comment reaches the order through CommentSalesConnector, which renders .comment-wrapper from spy_comment joined to spy_comment_thread on owner_type sales_order. The spec asserts .comment-wrapper. The test builds its own cart rather than selecting the named fixture quote: checkout consumes the cart, so on a retry the fixture cart no longer exists and the failure surfaces at selectCart, masking the real one. ProductAddToCartScenario adds to the active cart instead, which every attempt can do. Not ported: the source's explicit multi-cart creation and its named cart, which the three add-comment tests above already exercise, and its Zed admin login by shared-permission owner, replaced by the fixture rootUser.
target_test: given a cart carrying a comment when the order is placed then the comment is on the order in the storefront and in the back office

contract.journey: Configurable product checkout

name: Configurable_Product_Checkout
rationale: Duplicate journey — retired by the port of product/Configurable_Product_Checkout; delete it in that sibling's batch, it needs no port of its own.

contract.journey: Guest checkout with bundles, discounts and OMS.

name: Guest_Checkout
rationale: Delta only: guest checkout is covered by basic-checkout.cy.ts and the OMS tail by dummy-payment-oms-flow.cy.ts; what is left is the bundle plus voucher and cart-rule discounts in a guest cart. The row read AUTHORED/PRESENT before this batch only because it carried a target_path with no target_test, and scan.py reports PRESENT as soon as the file exists — the one test in that spec covers a logged-in customer with no bundle, so the guest delta was unwritten. It is now a second test in the same spec, and target_test names it. The fixture gained a three-product bundle: the carrier product is created first but priced and stocked only after haveProductBundle, keyed off the returned #productBundle, which is the ordering the working reorder-product-bundles fixture uses; pricing the carrier before bundling leaves it unaddable and the cart silently empty. The cart is built through ProductAddToCartScenario rather than a hand-rolled catalog search, so each repository takes its own path — quick-add by SKU on the b2b-style shops, catalog search plus PDP on the b2c-style ones. Not ported: the source's per-state OMS walk (skip grace period, Pay, Skip timeout, skip picking, Ship, Stock update, Close), which dummy-payment-oms-flow.cy.ts already covers, and the source's back-office discount deactivation teardown, which the spec's existing after() hook already performs for all three seeded discounts.
target_test: given a guest cart holding a product bundle when a voucher and a cart rule both collect then both discounts apply and the guest order is placed

contract.journey: Guest checkout with different addresses and OMS.

name: Guest_Checkout_Addresses
rationale: Delta only: the multi-shipment guest flow is covered; what is left is three distinct per-item delivery addresses and the back-office address assertions. target_path moved off basic-checkout.cy.ts, where the row previously pointed, to split-delivery.cy.ts. The reason is the fixtures: this delta needs three products plus a rootUser to read the order back in the back office, and split-delivery's fixture already carries exactly that, identically across all five repository variants, while the five basic-checkout fixtures have diverged - the mp ones build product offers and share none of the product1WithPrice/product3 keys - so landing it there would have meant five hand-diverged fixture edits for a journey that only b2c and suite run. It also sits with its sibling: the file's other test asserts the shipment count for a logged-in customer, and this asserts the addresses for a guest. Reading the order back needed a new handle. A guest has no order history, so CustomerOverviewPage.viewLastPlacedOrder cannot be used - it looks for the customer order table and times out. The order-success page carries the reference only as schema.org metadata, so CheckoutSummaryPage.getPlacedOrderReference reads meta[itemprop=identifier]; that is the only handle a guest has on the order it just placed. The address assertion is on distinctness, not on literal values: fillMultiShippingAddress generates each address internally with faker and returns nothing, so the spec asserts three delivery-address blocks whose texts are three distinct strings, which is what the source proved by filling three different streets. SalesDetailRepository gained getShipmentDeliveryAddresses for it; ShipmentGui renders the address as a plain p led by a bold 'Delivery Address:' label with no data-qa, so the label is the selector. Not ported: the source's per-shipment named shipping-method choice (Standard, Express, Air Sonic) and its billing-address assertion. The shipment-method radios carry the method's position rather than its name and which method sits where depends on the store, the same reason the sibling row already records for not asserting named methods. Guest checkout is skipped on b2b and b2b-mp, which is storefront reality rather than a narrowing - those shops offer no guest checkout at all.
target_test: given a guest cart of three items when each item is given its own delivery address then the order is split into one shipment per address

contract.journey: Login during checkout

name: Login_during_checkout
rationale: New spec, shared with the Register_during_checkout sibling since both journeys start as a guest at the same checkout customer step. The step offers three forms at once - register, guest and login - and nothing in cypress-tests drove any of them but the guest one, so CheckoutCustomerPage gained loginDuringCheckout and registerDuringCheckout and all five repositories gained the selectors. Worth recording: both the guest and the register form are nested one level deeper than their own form classes suggest. GuestForm and RegisterForm declare their fields directly under block prefixes guestForm and registerForm, but the checkout step wraps each in a parent form under a customer child, so the rendered ids are registerForm_customer_salutation and the like, not registerForm_salutation. The login form is not wrapped and stays loginForm_email. The proceed-as-registered-user toggler carries the id register, so its selector reads checkoutProceedAs register even though it reveals the login form too. After logging in the spec re-enters checkout from the cart rather than continuing in place; now that the customer is authenticated that lands on the address step, which is the same journey with one extra navigation. Not ported: the source's read-back of the last placed order id, which asserts nothing beyond the order-placed message the spec already checks.
target_test: given a guest cart when the customer logs in at the checkout customer step then the order is placed on that account

contract.journey: Checks that order with products and offers of multiple merchants could be placed and it will be split per merchant.

name: Multiple_Merchants_Order
rationale: Now locally proven. Two fixture defects were in the way, both mine rather than the stack's. The first: haveProductInStockForStore was applied only to the plain product, so the two offer-bearing concretes had no product-level stock and therefore no product availability at all - an offer's own stock does not produce it. The second and harder: offer availability published as zero because Pyz registers three product-offer-availability publisher plugins, driven by SpyProductOfferStore, SpyStock and SpyStockStore events, and none driven by SpyProductOfferStock. Writing the offer's stock therefore never republishes its availability, and all three registered triggers fire before the fixture writes that stock. Saving the offer-to-store relation afterwards with haveProductOfferStore fires an event that recomputes it with the stock in place, and availability comes out correct. The cart is arranged through the storefront API rather than the UI, and before the browser session exists. Only the API can put a named offer on an item: quick-add by SKU adds the plain product, which was verified - with availability fixed, quick-adding all three succeeds but the cart shows no Sold by line for either merchant - and havePersistentQuote discards the offer references its items carry. The product detail page is the only UI that can pick an offer and it is reachable solely through catalog search, which this stack cannot serve. The offer is this journey's premise rather than its subject: what is under test is the per-merchant split and the checkout. Filling the cart before login matters, because doing it after leaves the storefront on a different, empty cart. Assertions follow the source: the cart names the merchant behind each offer via Sold by, and the placed order carries one shipment per merchant, read as the count of ShipmentGui's per-shipment item tables. Not ported: the source's per-merchant price comparison on the PDP before choosing an offer, and its named per-shipment shipping methods, for the reason a sibling row records - the shipment radios carry the method's position rather than its name.
target_test: given a cart holding the main merchant product and an offer from each of two merchants when the order is placed then it is split into one shipment per merchant

contract.journey: Guest user email should be whitelisted from the AWS side before running the test.

name: Register_during_checkout
rationale: Second test of the checkout-authentication spec its Login_during_checkout sibling opens. The confirmation step is the substance of this row: this project enables double opt-in (both Pyz CustomerConfig and Pyz CustomerPageConfig return true from isDoubleOptInEnabled), so a freshly registered account cannot authenticate until it is confirmed, and a port that skipped confirmation would stall at the login. The source read the registration_key straight out of spy_customer with a SQL query and posted it to Glue /customer-confirmation. The port uses cy.confirmCustomerByEmail, a dynamic-fixture helper that already existed in this repository, which is the same effect through a supported entry point and needs no database access from the spec. The registration email was considered and not needed: the stack runs Mailpit and cypress.config.ts already exposes mailCatcherUrl, so extracting the confirmation link from the mail is possible, but the helper is the shorter honest path. The registration email address is built inside the test rather than at module scope, so a Cypress retry cannot reuse an address the previous attempt already registered. The profile read-back is ported: the spec asserts first name, last name and email on the customer profile form, which needed a public getEmailInput on CustomerProfilePage since only the internal updateEmail used it. Not ported: the source's teardown deleting the customer, which no Cypress fixture mechanism needs, and its salutation assertion, dropped because the profile select is asserted by the three identifying fields instead.
target_test: given a guest cart when the customer registers at the checkout customer step then the account is created and the order is placed on it

contract.journey: Checks user can request and receive quote.

name: Request_for_Quote
rationale: New spec and a new QuoteRequestPage page object - nothing for quote requests existed in cypress-tests, and the QuoteRequestPage and QuoteRequestAgentPage modules carry two data-qa hooks between them, so the routes are the handles: the cart's /quote-request/create link, the /quote-request/send-to-user/<ref> link which is also where the reference is read from, /agent/quote-request/revise/<ref>, and /quote-request/convert-to-cart/<ref>. The agent price field is quote_request_agent_form_latestVersion_quote_items_0_sourceUnitGrossPrice, guarded by a use_default_price checkbox that has to be cleared before a custom price is taken. The agent is a Zed user with is_agent true logging in at /agent/login, and the customer's cookies must be cleared first or that route redirects away. The price assertion is the part worth recording. Written body-wide it was vacuous: the cart prints the original price alongside the revised one, so asserting the page contained the revised price passed even when the expected value was changed to the original. It is now scoped to the cart summary and asserted both ways, contains the revised price and does not contain the original, and the revision was independently confirmed in spy_quote_request_version, whose latest row carries sourceUnitGrossPrice 25000 against a seeded 30000. The cart is built through the storefront rather than seeded: havePersistentQuote's quote is superseded by the company-user cart the storefront creates, so a seeded cart is not the one the journey acts on. Not ported: the second agent round trip, the customer's edit-items and note steps, and the valid-till date. The source runs the revise cycle twice and edits the request in between; the port keeps one cycle, which is what proves the mechanism - request, agent revision, conversion at the revised price - and drops the repetition and the note. Recorded here so the cutover does not read this row as covering item removal from a quote request or the note field.
target_test: given a quote request sent to an agent when the agent revises the item price then the customer converts it to a cart and orders at the revised price

contract.journey: Checks split delivery in checkout.

name: Split_Delivery
rationale: Delta only: multi-shipment checkout was already covered, but only as far as the order being placed. What the Robot test ended on was unchecked - three items to three addresses become three shipments. ShipmentGui renders one order-item table per shipment, so counting them is the shipment count. Named per-shipment shipping methods are not asserted: the radio ids carry the method's position rather than its name, and which method sits where depends on the store.
target_test: should create one shipment per delivery address when the cart is split

contract.journey: Create a new company user on Storefront.

name: Create_new_company_user_with_linked_entities_in_storefront
rationale: Two new storefront page objects, business unit create and company user create, plus the impersonation support the agent-assist row introduced. The company, its roles and the agent are seeded; the business unit and the company user are driven through the storefront, which is what the row is about. The created user's role grants company users and nothing else, so the company-role page has to refuse it, and impersonation is how that user can be driven at all given nothing knows its password.
target_test: company administrator should be able to create a business unit and a company user in it

name: Create_new_company_with_linked_entities_and_customer_in_backoffice

contract.journey: Add comments in Yves and check in Zed.

name: Comment_Management_in_Order
rationale: Delta only, and a narrower delta than the verdict's original note suggested. cart-comments.cy.ts already carries a comment written on the cart through checkout and reads it back on the storefront order details page and in the back office. What no spec covered is the source's own path: a comment written on the order itself, after it was placed, through the CommentThreadWidget the order details page mounts with owner type sales_order — a different thread from the quote-owned one the cart writes and checkout copies. The comment thread is a single widget rendered on both pages, so CommentCartPage drives it here rather than a duplicate page family with identical selectors; the sibling spec already reads the order page through that page object. The back-office half asserts on CommentSalesConnector's `.comment-wrapper` box, not on Sales' own `.order-details-chat`, which reads spy_sales_order_comment and no storefront comment ever lands in. Narrowed to the company-account storefronts, which is the source's own variant set. Not ported: the source's named multi-cart, which the journey does not depend on — the comment is written on the order, not on the cart it came from. The fixture seeds one persistent quote per configured attempt, because checkout consumes a cart and a Cypress retry would otherwise die on an empty one.
target_test: given a placed order when the customer comments on it in the storefront then the comment is shown there and in the back office

contract.journey: Checks create/edit shipment functions from backoffice.

name: Manage_Shipments
rationale: New spec. Back-office shipment CRUD was uncovered: split-delivery.cy.ts proves checkout produces one shipment per delivery address, but nothing created or edited a shipment from the back office. One journey, because the halves are not independent — the shipment the edit half corrects is the one the create half made. The order is placed to a single address so it starts as one shipment, then a second is created for one item with a fresh address and a shipment method picked out of the select's own options rather than named, and the item is asserted to have left the first shipment's table and joined the second's. Two things the source got wrong or never reached, both recorded in the run's learnings. Its `edit xxx shipment inside the order` keyword waits for the shipment's edit link and then clicks the create link, so it creates a third shipment instead of editing the second — which is why the source asserts three shipments and leaves shipment 2 untouched, and why editing was never actually covered. This port drives the real edit page, and the order stays at two shipments because the form carries form.shipment.idSalesShipment and updates in place. Second, ShipmentFormDataProvider hydrates the shipment's address but not its method, so the edit form comes up on the placeholder option and a required-field validation failure keeps the save on the form; the spec picks a method again on edit, which the comment above that step explains. Asserted on the address line and the shipment's own item table rather than the source's demo money and demo shipment-method names (EUR 785.90, 'Spryker Drone Shipment - Air Light'), so the fixture owns everything it checks. Not ported: the source's deactivate-all-discounts setup and re-activation teardown, which are destructive to every spec sharing the environment, its multi-address checkout that collapsed back into one shipment anyway because all three addresses were identical, and the requested delivery date, whose only source value is a fixed past date that would age.
target_test: given an order delivered as one shipment when a second shipment is created and then edited then the item moves and the edited address is kept

contract.journey: Check that customer is able to cancel order.

name: Order_Cancellation
rationale: New spec. Ported as two journeys off one source test: the customer cancelling an order whose items are all cancellable, and the same order refusing to offer cancellation once one item has left the cancellable states. Those are the two halves the source alternates between, and they are independent, so they are separate it()s rather than one long chain. OrderCancelButtonWidget renders its form only while OrderExpander::setOrderIsCancellableByItemState finds the cancellable flag on every item's state, so the button is absent from the DOM rather than hidden, and both halves assert on existence. The five yves order-details repositories gained getCancelOrderButton and the back-office SalesDetailPage gained triggerOmsForOrderItem, which is what lets the second journey advance one item and leave the other where it was; the existing triggerOms drives the whole order and cannot express that. Note the item-level buttons are labelled ucfirst() of the event name while the order-level box prints the raw name, so the same event reads 'Skip grace period' on the row and 'skip grace period' on the order box. Not ported: the source's address bookkeeping and its second, identical assertion after advancing the remaining item, which adds no coverage over the first.
target_test: given every item of an order is cancellable when the customer cancels it then the order is cancelled

contract.journey: Checks that refund can be created for one item and the whole order.

name: Refunds
rationale: Delta only: refund-management.cy.ts covers the list page and a single-item refund reached through a return, so what is left is the source's own path — refunding a delivered item directly, per item, and the order's grand total walking down to zero. DummyRefund01 offers `refund` from both `returned` and `delivered`; the sibling spec drives the first, this one drives the second, which is why the order has to walk the whole happy path to `delivered` first. Kept as one test rather than two, because the halves are not independent: the second refunds the remainder of the same order the first refunded one item of, which is exactly what the contract sentence 'for one item and the whole order' describes. The item total is read before the refund is triggered — the recalculation that follows writes the item's canceled amount and the row then reports what is left to pay. Asserted on the raw minor-unit amounts the item, refund and total blocks publish rather than the source's demo-data money strings (EUR 1,041.90 / 696.90 / 0.00), so the fixture prices the three products itself; the final state is the same claim, that the grand total is zero and the refunds sum to what the order originally cost. Narrowed away from the marketplace shops: MarketplacePayment01 reaches `refunded` only from `cancelled` and has no `Stock update`, so the delivered-to-refunded transition does not exist there — the same narrowing refund-management.cy.ts already carries. Not ported: the source's deactivate-all-discounts setup and its re-activation teardown, which are destructive to every other spec sharing the environment; fixture-priced products with no discount attached make them unnecessary.
target_test: given a delivered order of three items when they are refunded one by one then each refund is recorded and the grand total reaches zero

contract.journey: Checks that returns work and oms process is checked.

name: Return_Management
rationale: New spec, scoped to the storefront half the row's target path names. The source is one very long test that walks four surfaces — the storefront return, the merchant portal's Execute return, a back-office return on a third item, and an agent-assist login creating a return on behalf of the customer — and only the first of those is a yves journey. What is ported is the customer's own return: a shipped order of three items, two of them returned from the order details page, and the OMS half the documentation calls out. `start-return` is not a manual event, so creating the return is what moves those two items out of `shipped` on its own; the spec asserts both states are present afterwards, which is what shows the item left out of the return did not move. Reaching a returnable state at all needs the order walked to `shipped` first, since DummyReturn01 offers `start-return` from `shipped` and `delivered` only. The return line's checkbox is checked forcibly: SalesReturnPage renders a styled control whose real input is covered by CSS, the same shape the cart-reorder checkboxes already carry. Assertions are on the fixture's own SKUs and on the two OMS state labels, never on demo products. Not ported here: the print slip, which lists the same items the return details page already shows, and the merchant-portal, back-office and agent-assist halves, which belong to their own surfaces rather than to this row's yves contract. Also not ported: the source's delete-all-addresses teardown and the throwaway Zed agent user it creates and deletes, both of which exist only to serve the agent-assist half.
target_test: given a shipped order of three items when the customer returns two of them then only those move to waiting for return

name: Discounts
rationale: Delta only: discount-create.cy.ts and discount-list.cy.ts cover back-office CRUD; what is left is the whole storefront half - amounts in the cart, the promo product and the checkout total. The three discounts are therefore seeded by fixture rather than driven through the back-office forms, which would re-cover what those two specs already do: haveDiscount takes a nested discountGeneral/discountCalculator override, and the promotional product needs no extra helper because DiscountPromotionPostCreatePlugin is wired in Pyz and persists the promotion as soon as collectorStrategyType is 'promotion'. Asserted by display name and voucher code read back out of the fixture response, not by amount: the source's exact minus-amounts were already replaced with partial matches upstream for dump-restore tolerance, and names are unique per run while amounts are not, so a leftover discount from an earlier run cannot make the assertion pass. The promotional product is added by its own sku, because any other active promotion discount offers its product in the same carousel. The source opened with 'deactivate all discounts in the database'; that is not ported, because it is destructive to every other spec sharing the environment. The narrower version closes the spec instead - the teardown deactivates the three discounts this run seeded, through the discount list's Deactivate action, which is a form button rather than a link. Known cost: a run that dies before the teardown leaves those three active, and collector query strings cannot be scoped to the fixture's own sku because a fixture reference only resolves as a whole value, never inside a larger string.
target_test: given a cart rule, a voucher and a promotional product discount when the voucher is redeemed and the promotional product is added then all three are applied and the order is placed

contract.journey: checks that global minimum and maximum order thresholds can be applied.

name: Minimum_Order_Value
rationale: No Cypress spec covers this journey - author a new one. Ported as one journey, because the source is one test whose halves are not independent: the cart has to be above the maximum for the block to mean anything, and below it for the order to prove the fee survives to checkout. Three deliberate departures from the source. First, the product is created and priced by the fixture at 300.00 instead of reusing demo SKUs, so the thresholds can be stated as absolute amounts; the source's exact grand total of 83.90 was derived from a demo price point, and that is the same coupling the sibling Discounts test already had to strip for dump-restore tolerance. The exact 9.00 surcharge is asserted instead, in the cart and on the summary, which is the configured fee rather than a demo-data artefact. Second, the cart crosses the maximum by changing the quantity rather than by removing a second line: the quote is seeded once per spec and a Cypress retry re-runs the test against whatever the previous attempt left in it, so an absolute quantity is the only arrange step that means the same thing on every attempt. Third, the second pass through checkout skips the address step - changing the quantity invalidates the shipment step, so the checkout resumes there and never asks for the address again; CheckoutScenario gained a shouldSkipAddressStep flag beside the shouldSkipShipmentStep and shouldSkipPlaceOrder flags it already had. The source's back-office grand-total check is not ported: the row's contract is the yves surface, and the surcharge is asserted on the summary the order is placed from. Proving this locally needed an environment repair, not a spec change - see the run's learnings for the missing CustomerAccess installer data.
target_test: given global order thresholds when the cart is above the maximum and then below it then checkout is blocked and the soft threshold fee is charged

contract.journey: DMS-ON: https://spryker.atlassian.net/browse/FRW-7396.

name: Data_exchange_API_Configuration_in_Zed
rationale: Only creating the mime-types dynamic-entity configuration is a browser journey; the assertions are POST, PATCH and GET calls with response-body checks. Keep the configuration form as a Cypress spec and move the CRUD assertions to the Glue and back-office API suite. Regenerating the specification mid-test is available through cy.runCliCommands. The Cypress half asserts the form's own contract rather than the API's: the configuration is enabled, every field definition is configured, and the reloaded form renders back exactly the type and the creatable/editable/required flags that were saved. It does not regenerate the specification at all - that belongs to the download sibling, and leaving it out keeps this spec at 22s. The visible names carry a per-run marker, because every other value in this form is one an earlier run could have left behind: the sibling spec configures the same five fields of the same table, so asserting the plain values alone would pass against untouched state and prove nothing this run did. Teardown disables the configuration instead of deleting the row, which Cypress has no route to, so both data-exchange specs converge on is_active = 0 and the sibling's baseline - the schema does not expose /mime-types - still holds. Verified: the two specs are green in one run together, in both orders, and the database shows the row disabled afterwards.
target_test: given a data exchange api configuration for a table when its resource fields are configured and saved then the reloaded form renders back what was saved

name: Data_exchange_API_download_specification
rationale: No Cypress spec covers this journey - author a new one. Regenerating the specification mid-test is available: cy.runCliCommands posts cli-command operations to the dynamic-fixtures endpoint, which runs them in the application container, and the isFileExists task plus cy.readFile cover inspecting the downloaded file. Ported as one journey, because the source is one test and its halves are not independent: the baseline download proves spy_mime_type is absent, and only then does enabling its configuration prove the specification gained /mime-types. The forced form of the command (no --invalidated-after-interval) is used, so generation never no-ops on the voter; the scheduled job keeps the interval. The download button carries class 'disabled' while the stored schema is older than any configuration row, which is the stale-schema assertion, and cy.reloadUntilGone re-runs generation on every reload to converge past the same-second race between a save and a regeneration. A deleteFile task was added beside isFileExists so the second download lands as schema.yml again instead of 'schema (1).yml' - the source deleted the file between downloads for the same reason. The configuration is reached through the create form's option list rather than the edit URL: the create data provider offers only unconfigured tables, so its options are a clean create-or-edit discriminator, and the edit URL answers 500 for a table that exists but has no configuration. Teardown disables the configuration and regenerates instead of deleting the row, which Cypress has no route to; the spec is green on both the create and the edit path.
target_test: given a table is not exposed when its data exchange api configuration is enabled and the specification is regenerated then the downloaded specification gains its resource

contract.journey: DMS-ON: https://spryker.atlassian.net/browse/FRW-7463.

name: Fulfillment_app_e2e
rationale: The browser is incidental: only the warehouse-user checkbox and a few back-office OMS clicks are UI, while order creation, warehouse assignment and the whole picking start-and-pick flow are Glue and back-office API calls plus direct database updates. Split into an API picking test plus this thin back-office spec. The spec keeps the two UI halves the source actually drove: setting the warehouse-user flag on the user form, asserted through the Assign Warehouses row action the flag unlocks, and the OMS walk from a fixture order to `ready for picking` via the `picking list generation schedule` event. target_test names the second; the first is "should offer the warehouse assignment action when a back-office user is flagged as a warehouse user". Runs for suite, b2c and b2c-mp only — b2b and b2b-mp do not wire WarehouseUserGui. The picking OMS walk runs on suite only: haveFullOrder ships in spryker-feature/self-service-portal and haveShipmentType/haveShipmentMethod are registered in suite's dynamic-fixture suite alone. b2c-demo-shop and b2c-demo-marketplace do register the core SprykerTest\Shared\Sales\Helper\SalesDataHelper that suite itself omits, so they can build a bare order through haveOrder — what they cannot build is its shipment, and ShipmentGui renders the order items per shipment group, so widening the walk to them needs a shipment-building path first. The warehouse-user flag test still runs on all three. The order's stock must be a warehouse that carries a picking_list_strategy: haveProductInStockForStore builds its stock through haveStock, which persists only the name, so the strategy lands NULL and the generate-picking-lists onEnter command throws inside requirePickingListStrategy, parking the item in picking list generation scheduled with no error the spec can see. The fixture therefore builds the stock explicitly through haveStock plus haveStockProduct against the demodata Warehouse1, whose multi-shipment strategy is the only generator strategy Pyz registers. No warehouse-user assignment is needed to reach ready for picking; that is only required to pick as a user. The source waits for two order items to reach ready for picking; the port waits for one, because haveFullOrder builds a strictly single-item order — SalesDataHelper::createQuoteTransfer calls withItem() once and the override key is `item`, singular — so a second item needs a quote-building path this reshape does not add. The it() title names one item to match.
target_test: should move the order item to ready for picking when picking list generation is scheduled
